<reason>A close, high-quality debate. PRO built a coherent case (bans export demand, payment respects labor, regulation splits enforceable from unenforceable terms) and landed the "need is not coercion or every wage is coercion" pressure, which CON never fully dissolved. But CON did more damage with turns on PRO's own material: the screening criterion as an admission that payment recruits; PRO's own description of surrogates wanting "high, time-limited pay" as proof the pay is the driver; and flipping PRO's "ongoing consent" kidney distinction against pre-birth parentage orders where consent effectively ends at conception. CON also handled the sharpest pressure question honestly (conceding the rare case where an altruistic surrogate keeps the child) and reframed it as ordinary adoption law, while noting the cross-border scandal jurisdictions PRO blamed on bans were legal paid markets. PRO's "that was under-regulation" reply was fair under the motion's wording but weaker than CON's turn. CON's closing crystallized the decisive question (whose claim the state enforces and why) more cleanly than PRO's concession-focused closing. Costs to CON: the clipped final turn and the unresolved proves-too-much point keep the margin thin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 turning PRO's own A1/A2 answers: the surrogate motivated by "high, time-limited pay" shows the price recruits even after screening, and "ongoing consent" cannot coexist with a pre-birth order that fixes parentage before the child exists, so unlike the kidney donor "she keeps nothing, by court order, because money changed hands."</best_rebuttal>
